Chapter 56 - Architecture Requirements, Trade-offs, and ADRs
From ambiguous business goals to reviewable technical decisions
Learning Objectives

Translate business outcomes into functional and non-functional requirements.

Use constraints, quality attributes, risk analysis, and architectural decision records.

Compare alternatives using measurable trade-offs rather than service preference. Why This Matters in Production
Poor architecture usually begins before the first resource is created: unclear objectives, hidden assumptions, and
unowned risks. Senior engineers make uncertainty explicit and preserve the reasoning behind consequential
decisions. Production principle Architecture is a sequence of reversible and irreversible decisions. Document context,
alternatives, consequences, and validation evidence before complexity becomes institutional memory. Working Backward from Outcomes
Start with customer and business outcomes, then derive measurable requirements. Separate mandatory constraints
from preferences. Define workload scope, users, data classification, traffic shape, availability targets, recovery
objectives, compliance needs, delivery timeline, team capability, and budget. Quality attribute



Stretch challenge Revisit the decision after changing one constraint, such as data residency or 10x traffic, and
write a superseding ADR. Chapter Summary

Requirements and quality attributes make architecture reviewable.




1. What makes an architecture decision significant?
It materially affects structure, security, reliability, data, interfaces, cost, or future change and is expensive or risky

2. Why record rejected alternatives?
They prevent repeated debate and show that the selected decision was made against explicit constraints.
3. When should an ADR be reviewed?
When assumptions, constraints, service capabilities, incidents, risk, or business outcomes materially change. Official AWS References

Chapter 57 - Enterprise SaaS Architecture
Tenant isolation, identity, metering, onboarding, and noisy-neighbor control
Learning Objectives

Compare pooled, siloed, and bridge tenant-isolation models.

Design tenant-aware identity, authorization, data partitioning, observability, and metering.

Build onboarding, offboarding, deployment, and support processes for multi-tenant systems. Why This Matters in Production
SaaS architecture is not simply a shared web application. Every control plane and data plane must carry tenant
context, enforce isolation, expose tenant-level health and cost, and support lifecycle automation. Production principle Tenant identity must be established once, propagated explicitly, and enforced at every
resource and data-access boundary. Never rely on a user-supplied tenant identifier alone. Isolation Models

Use an identity provider and trusted claims to establish tenant context. Authorizers or application middleware
convert identity into an internal tenant principal. Partition keys, row-level controls, schemas, databases, buckets,
queues, caches, and logs must preserve that context. Test for cross-tenant access as a first-class security requirement. Operations and Economics



Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. What is a noisy neighbor?
A tenant whose usage consumes disproportionate shared capacity and degrades other tenants.
2. How do you prevent tenant spoofing?
Derive tenant context from trusted authentication and authorization claims, then ignore or validate client-supplied
tenant values.
3. When should a tenant be siloed?
When regulation, performance, contractual isolation, customization, or blast-radius requirements justify dedicated
resources. Official AWS References

Chapter 58 - Hybrid Connectivity and Migration Waves
Discovery, landing zones, Direct Connect, VPN, DNS, identity, and cutover control
Learning Objectives

Create an assess-mobilize-migrate plan with application dependencies and wave governance.

Design resilient hybrid connectivity, routing, DNS, identity, and security inspection.

Execute cutovers with replication, testing, rollback, and business communication. Why This Matters in Production
Enterprise migrations fail when teams move servers without moving dependencies, operations, identity, or
ownership. Hybrid architecture must support coexistence for months or years while remaining observable and
secure. Production principle Migrate applications as dependency-aware products, not as isolated servers. Every wave
needs acceptance criteria, rollback, owner readiness, and measured business impact. Discovery and Portfolio Planning
Inventory applications, servers, databases, interfaces, data flows, owners, criticality, compliance, lifecycle, and cost. Group systems by dependency and business process. Select migration strategies such as rehost, replatform, refactor,
repurchase, retain, relocate, or retire. Hybrid Network Design

Chapter 59 - Application Modernization and Monolith
Decomposition
Strangler patterns, domain boundaries, data migration, and coexistence
Learning Objectives

Assess whether to retain, replatform, modularize, or decompose a monolith.

Apply strangler fig, branch by abstraction, anti-corruption layer, and event-driven integration patterns.

Manage data ownership, consistency, deployment, observability, and organizational change. Why This Matters in Production
Microservices are not an objective. Modernization should improve a measurable constraint such as delivery speed,
scalability, resilience, maintainability, or technology lifecycle. Poor decomposition creates distributed complexity
without business value. Production principle Decompose around stable business capabilities and team ownership. Migrate incrementally
with reversible coexistence, measurable outcomes, and explicit data authority. Modernization Assessment
Measure current deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time, lead time, scaling constraints, defect
concentration, coupling, ownership, and technology risk. A well-structured modular monolith can be better than
premature microservices. Incremental Patterns

An incremental modernization approach in which new capabilities are built around and gradually replace parts of

Chapter 60 - Multi-Region and Global Application Design
Latency, sovereignty, failover, data replication, and operational independence
Learning Objectives

Choose active-passive, active-active, or partitioned global architectures.

Design DNS, traffic, identity, data, secrets, observability, and deployment across Regions.

Define failover authority, consistency, data residency, and recovery testing. Why This Matters in Production

survive not only infrastructure loss but control-plane isolation, stale data, partial replication, operator confusion, and
unsafe failback. Production principle Use multi-Region only when business objectives justify its ongoing cost and complexity. Each Region should be as operationally independent as the recovery objective requires. Global Architecture Patterns

Chapter Summary

Multi-Region architecture trades regional resilience for system complexity.

Traffic, data, identity, security, observability, and operations all require regional design.

1. Active-active or active-passive: which is better?
Neither universally; choose based on RTO, RPO, consistency, traffic, operational capability, and cost.
2. Why can DNS failover be slow or unsafe?
Caching, resolver behavior, shallow health checks, and stale sessions can delay or misdirect traffic.
